chunks: From him, from Ahmad ibn Abi Bishr, from Muawiya ibn Maythara, who said: I heard Abu al-Jarud ask Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

About a man who sold his house to another man, and there was a mortgage/encumbrance between him and the buyer. He stipulated: 'If you bring me my money within three years, the house is yours.' He brought him his money. The Imam said: 'He has his condition (the right to redeem).' Abu al-Jarud said to him: 'That man has acquired/kept that money within three years.' He said: 'It is his money.' And Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'What do you think if the house burned down? Whose money was it? The house belongs to the buyer.'

key_terms.الدَّارُ دَارَ الْمُشْتَرِي: The house belongs to the buyer; indicating ownership transfer or risk bearing.
key_terms.حَاصِرٌ: Mortgage or encumbrance; a right of redemption or lien on a property.
key_terms.شَرْطُهُ: His condition; the stipulation made in the contract remains valid and binding.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a conditional sale with a right of redemption in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) validates the *shart* (condition) in a sale where the buyer retains the property if the seller fails to repay within three years, effectively treating the unpaid sum as the price of the house. The Imam’s rhetorical question regarding the house burning down clarifies that risk of loss (*ghurm*) follows the right of ownership (*ghinm*), a foundational principle in Shia jurisprudence for conditional sales (*mu'atah*). This ruling underscores the flexibility of contractual stipulations in Shia fiqh, provided they do not contradict the essence of the transaction.
